A close reading for the week

“So we beat on”

The Great Gatsby · the last page

On his last night in the East, Nick Carraway sits on Gatsby’s beach and watches the moon rise until the houses disappear. What he sees in their place is the oldest American sight there is, and the reason Gatsby’s dream was doomed before he dreamed it.

And as the moon rose higher the inessential houses began to melt away until gradually I became aware of the old island here that flowered once for Dutch sailors’ eyes—a fresh, green breast of the new world.1 Its vanished trees, the trees that had made way for Gatsby’s house, had once pandered in whispers to the last and greatest of all human dreams; for a transitory enchanted moment man must have held his breath in the presence of this continent,2 compelled into an aesthetic contemplation he neither understood nor desired, face to face for the last time in history with something commensurate to his capacity for wonder.

  1. 1

    The continent as a body

    With the houses imagined away, Nick sees Long Island as the Dutch sailors of the 1600s saw it: fresh, green, a “breast”: the new world as nurture, promise, a body offering itself to the arriving eye. The image gives America’s discovery the shape of desire, which is what allows the paragraph to fuse it, a few lines later, with one man’s longing across a bay.

  2. 2

    The held breath

    ‘Transitory’ admits it straight away: the enchanted moment was already passing as it happened. The sailors are “compelled” into contemplation they “neither understood nor desired”: wonder arriving unwanted, before commerce resumed. Fitzgerald’s history is elegy from the first glance: the trees that pandered to the dream were cut down for houses like Gatsby’s.
